::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** 60 to 90 minutes, at home, any time; best before [lesson 02](02-project-organization.qmd).
- **You need:** a terminal ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd#open-a-terminal): macOS Terminal, a Linux terminal, or Ubuntu in WSL2 on Windows). Pixi only for the ShellCheck step.
- **You will have:** a practice folder with a sample sheet, three small FASTQ files and `count_reads.sh`, a script that counts reads.
- **Cheat sheet:** [Bash](../cheatsheets/bash.qmd)
:::

## Overview

Every lesson in this course is typed into a terminal, where a program called
the **shell** reads your commands and runs them. This page practises the
commands the lessons use, in a folder of its own, on files you make yourself,
so nothing you do here can harm your other work. Type the commands rather
than pasting them: your fingers learn them faster than your eyes.

If you have used a terminal before, go straight to
[*Try it yourself*](#try-it-yourself) and check whether you can answer the
questions.

::: {.callout-note title="Bash or zsh?"}
The terminal on macOS runs **zsh**; Linux and WSL2 run **bash**. Both are
shells, and every command on this page works in both. Scripts (section 8)
always run with bash, because their first line asks for it. The one
difference that matters here is explained in the [*Break it*](#break-it-spaces-in-file-names).
:::

### Learning outcomes

After this page you can:

1. **Move** between folders and **use** paths relative to where you are.
2. **Create**, look into, copy, move and delete files and folders.
3. **Combine** commands with pipes and redirection to answer a question about a data file.
4. **Repeat** a command over many files with a loop, and **save** it as a script you run with one command.

Checks: your answers to *Try it yourself*, and `count_reads.sh` printing the
read counts of all three files.

## 1. Where am I?

The shell always works *in* a folder, the **working directory**. Ask which:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~
pwd
```

```text
/Users/ada
```

`~` is your **home** folder (on Linux `/home/ada`). `cd` (change directory)
moves you; `pwd` (print working directory) says where you are. Make a folder
for this page and go there:

```{.bash .run}
mkdir -p ~/cbio7501/bash-practice
cd ~/cbio7501/bash-practice
pwd
```

```text
/Users/ada/cbio7501/bash-practice
```

`mkdir -p` makes the folder and any missing folders above it, and does not
complain if it already exists.

A path that starts with `/` (or `~`) is **absolute**: it means the same thing
wherever you are. Any other path is **relative** to the working directory.
`..` means the folder above, `.` the folder you are in:

```{.bash .run}
cd ..
pwd
cd bash-practice
```

```text
/Users/ada/cbio7501
```

The lessons always work from the project folder with relative paths, so a
project still works after it moves ([lesson 02](02-project-organization.qmd#break-it-absolute-paths)).

## 2. Make some files

`echo` prints text; `>` sends it into a file instead of the screen
(**redirection**), and `>>` adds to the end of a file:

```{.bash .run}
echo "My first file" > notes.txt
echo "A second line" >> notes.txt
cat notes.txt
```

```text
My first file
A second line
```

Careful: `>` replaces the file without asking. `cat` prints a whole file.

Now make the practice data. First two folders, like a small project:

```{.bash .run}
mkdir -p data results
ls
```

```text
data  notes.txt  results
```

In your editor (or with the copy buttons), save this sample sheet as
`samples.tsv` in `bash-practice/`. Its columns are separated by tabs; it is a
short version of the LTEE sample sheet from [lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd#describe-the-samples):

```{.text filename="samples.tsv" .write}
sample	strain	generation	population	mutator	cit
SRR2589044	REL2181A	5000	Ara-3	None	unknown
SRR2584863	REL7179B	15000	Ara-3	None	unknown
SRR2584866	REL11365	50000	Ara-3	plus	plus
```

And three small FASTQ files in `data/`. FASTQ stores one read in four lines:
a name starting with `@`, the sequence, a `+`, and one quality letter per
base. These reads are made up for practice:

```{.text filename="data/SRR2589044.fastq" .write}
@SRR2589044.1
ACGTTGCAAGGCTTACGATC
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
@SRR2589044.2
TTGACCGTAGGCATCGATCA
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIHHHHGGGG
```

```{.text filename="data/SRR2584863.fastq" .write}
@SRR2584863.1
GGCATTACGTACGATCGGAA
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
@SRR2584863.2
CATCGGATTACAGGCT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
@SRR2584863.3
ATTGCCGATCGTTACGGACT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIHHHHHH
```

```{.text filename="data/SRR2584866.fastq" .write}
@SRR2584866.1
TTACGGCATCGATTACGCAT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
@SRR2584866.2
GCGCGATATCGCGATTACGA
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
@SRR2584866.3
ACGATCGGCT
+
IIIIIIIIII
@SRR2584866.4
TTGCAGGCATCGAATCGGCA
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII
```

## 3. Look into files

```{.bash .run}
ls -l data
```

```text
total 24
-rw-r--r--  1 ada  staff  166 Oct 25 10:00 SRR2584863.fastq
-rw-r--r--  1 ada  staff  212 Oct 25 10:00 SRR2584866.fastq
-rw-r--r--  1 ada  staff  116 Oct 25 10:00 SRR2589044.fastq
```

`ls -l` lists files with their permissions, owner, size in bytes and date.
For a first look at a data file, read only its start or end:

```{.bash .run}
head -n 2 samples.tsv
tail -n 1 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv data/SRR2584863.fastq
```

```text
sample	strain	generation	population	mutator	cit
SRR2589044	REL2181A	5000	Ara-3	None	unknown
SRR2584866	REL11365	50000	Ara-3	plus	plus
       4 samples.tsv
      12 data/SRR2584863.fastq
      16 total
```

`wc -l` counts lines: the sample sheet has a header and three samples, and
the FASTQ file has 12 lines, so 3 reads. (Linux prints the numbers without
the leading spaces.) `head -4 FILE.fastq` shows the first read of any FASTQ
file, as in [lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd#download-the-reads-and-check-them).

To scroll through a long file, use `less`; leave it with `q`:

```{.bash .norun}
less samples.tsv
```

## 4. Pick out what you need

`grep` prints the lines that contain a word; `-c` counts them instead, and
`-v` keeps the lines that do *not* match:

```{.bash .run}
grep SRR2584863 samples.tsv
grep -c Ara-3 samples.tsv
grep -v unknown samples.tsv
```

```text
SRR2584863	REL7179B	15000	Ara-3	None	unknown
3
sample	strain	generation	population	mutator	cit
SRR2584866	REL11365	50000	Ara-3	plus	plus
```

`cut` keeps columns (fields, separated by tabs): here the sample name and the
generation.

```{.bash .run}
cut -f 1,3 samples.tsv
```

```text
sample	generation
SRR2589044	5000
SRR2584863	15000
SRR2584866	50000
```

A `*` in a file name matches anything (a **wildcard**). The shell replaces
`data/*.fastq` with the list of matching files before the command runs:

```{.bash .run}
ls data/*.fastq
echo data/*.fastq
```

```text
data/SRR2584863.fastq data/SRR2584866.fastq data/SRR2589044.fastq
data/SRR2584863.fastq data/SRR2584866.fastq data/SRR2589044.fastq
```

## 5. Pipes: one command's output is the next one's input

The `|` (**pipe**) passes what one command prints to the next command. Which
values does the `cit` column (column 6) take, and how often? Take the column,
drop the header line, sort, and count identical neighbours:

```{.bash .run}
cut -f 6 samples.tsv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c
```

```text
   1 plus
   2 unknown
```

`tail -n +2` starts at line 2, so it drops the header. `uniq -c` only counts
lines that are next to each other, which is why `sort` comes first. Build a
pipe one command at a time, and look at the output after each step.

Save the answer in a file with `>`, as for `echo`:

```{.bash .run}
cut -f 6 samples.tsv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c > results/cit-counts.txt
cat results/cit-counts.txt
```

Two more pipes the lessons use: how many files, and which sample is the most
evolved (sort by column 3 as numbers, take the last line)?

```{.bash .run}
ls data/*.fastq | wc -l
tail -n +2 samples.tsv | sort -k3,3n | tail -n 1 | cut -f 1
```

```text
       3
SRR2584866
```

## 6. Copy, move, rename, delete

```{.bash .run}
cp samples.tsv samples-backup.tsv
mv samples-backup.tsv results/
ls results
mv results/samples-backup.tsv results/samples-copy.tsv
rm results/samples-copy.tsv
ls results
```

```text
cit-counts.txt  samples-backup.tsv
cit-counts.txt
```

`mv` both moves and renames. `rm` deletes **for good**: there is no trash
folder in the shell. `rm -r FOLDER` deletes a folder and everything in it, so
read the command twice before you press Enter. Files in Git can be brought
back ([lesson 04](04-git.qmd#break-it-delete-your-work-then-get-it-back)); other files cannot.

## 7. Variables and loops

A **variable** holds a value; `$` reads it. `$( ... )` puts a command's
output into the command line, and `$(( ... ))` does arithmetic:

```{.bash .run}
f=data/SRR2584863.fastq
echo "The file is $f"
lines=$(wc -l < "$f")
echo "It has $(( lines / 4 )) reads"
```

```text
The file is data/SRR2584863.fastq
It has 3 reads
```

No spaces around `=`. `wc -l < "$f"` reads the file through `<` so that `wc`
prints only the number, without the file name.

A `for` loop runs the same commands once for each item in a list. Count the
reads of every file:

```{.bash .run}
for f in data/*.fastq; do
    echo "$f: $(( $(wc -l < "$f") / 4 )) reads"
done
```

```text
data/SRR2584863.fastq: 3 reads
data/SRR2584866.fastq: 4 reads
data/SRR2589044.fastq: 2 reads
```

`basename` drops the folder and, if you give it, an ending; the lessons use
it to turn file names into sample names:

```{.bash .run}
basename data/SRR2584863.fastq .fastq
```

```text
SRR2584863
```

## 8. Your first script

Typing the loop again tomorrow is error-prone. Save it in a file, a
**script**, as `count_reads.sh` in `bash-practice/`:

```{.bash filename="count_reads.sh" .write}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Print the number of reads in each FASTQ file given on the command line.
# Usage: bash count_reads.sh data/*.fastq
set -euo pipefail

for f in "$@"; do
    reads=$(( $(wc -l < "$f") / 4 ))
    printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(basename "$f" .fastq)" "$reads"
done
```

- The first line (the **shebang**) says which program runs the file: bash.
- `set -euo pipefail` stops the script at the first error, at an unset
  variable, and at a failing command inside a pipe, instead of going on with
  wrong results. The pipeline script in [lesson 05](05-pixi.qmd#alignment-and-variant-calling) starts the same way.
- `"$@"` is the list of everything you typed after the script's name.

Run it:

```{.bash .run}
bash count_reads.sh data/*.fastq
```

```text
SRR2584863	3
SRR2584866	4
SRR2589044	2
```

To run it by its name, make it **executable** once, then save its output as a
table:

```{.bash .run}
chmod +x count_reads.sh
./count_reads.sh data/*.fastq > results/read-counts.tsv
cat results/read-counts.tsv
```

`./` means "in this folder": the shell does not look for programs in the
working directory unless you say so.

ShellCheck reads a script and points out common mistakes, such as missing
quotes. Run it through Pixi ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd)); no output means it
found nothing:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec shellcheck count_reads.sh
```

## 9. Permissions

The first column of `ls -l` shows who may **r**ead, **w**rite and e**x**ecute
a file: the owner, the group, everyone else.

```{.bash .run}
ls -l count_reads.sh data/SRR2589044.fastq
```

```text
-rwxr-xr-x  1 ada  staff  272 Oct 25 10:00 count_reads.sh
-rw-r--r--  1 ada  staff  116 Oct 25 10:00 data/SRR2589044.fastq
```

Raw data should be read-only, so that no command changes it by mistake
([lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd#make-raw-data-read-only)). Take away the
write permission, then try to add a line:

```{.bash .run}
chmod a-w data/*.fastq
```

```{.bash .expect-fail}
echo "oops" >> data/SRR2589044.fastq
```

```text
bash: data/SRR2589044.fastq: Permission denied
```

The file is safe. (`chmod u+w FILE` gives the write permission back.)

## Try it yourself

1. In which folder are you? List the files in `results/` without going there.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `pwd`, then `ls results`.
   :::

2. Which samples carry the mutator (column 5 is not `None`)? Print only their names.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `tail -n +2 samples.tsv | grep -v None | cut -f 1` prints `SRR2584866`.
   Careful: a plain `grep -v None` would also keep the header line.
   :::

3. How many bases are in `data/SRR2584866.fastq` in total? (The sequences are
   on lines 2, 6, 10, ...; `awk` can pick every fourth line and add up
   lengths.)

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `awk 'NR % 4 == 2 { n += length($0) } END { print n }' data/SRR2584866.fastq`
   prints `70` (20 + 20 + 10 + 20). `NR` is the line number in `awk`.
   :::

4. Change `count_reads.sh` so that it also prints the total number of reads at
   the end, then check it with ShellCheck.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   Before the loop add `total=0`; inside it, `total=$(( total + reads ))`;
   after `done`, `printf 'total\t%s\n' "$total"`. The output ends with
   `total	9`.
   :::

## Break it: spaces in file names

The shell splits a command line at spaces, so a file name with a space looks
like two names, unless it is in quotes. Make such a file and try to count its
lines, first without quotes:

```{.bash .run}
cp data/SRR2584863.fastq "my reads.fastq"
f="my reads.fastq"
```

Predict what happens, then run it:

```{.bash .expect-fail}
bash -c 'f="my reads.fastq"; wc -l $f'
```

```text
wc: my: open: No such file or directory
wc: reads.fastq: open: No such file or directory
       0 total
```

(Linux words the message a little differently.) Bash split `$f` into `my` and `reads.fastq`. With quotes it works:

```{.bash .run}
wc -l "$f"
rm "my reads.fastq"
```

(The command runs in `bash -c '...'` because zsh, the macOS terminal's shell,
does *not* split variables, so `wc -l $f` happens to work there. Scripts run
with bash, where it fails.) Two habits avoid the problem: put `"$f"` in quotes
every time, and never put spaces in file names
([lesson 02](02-project-organization.qmd#name-files-so-that-they-sort-and-explain-themselves)).

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `No such file or directory` | You are in another folder, or the name is misspelt. Check with `pwd` and `ls`; press `Tab` to complete names. |
| `Permission denied` when running a script | Run it with `bash script.sh`, or once `chmod +x script.sh`, then `./script.sh`. |
| `command not found` | A typo, or the program is not installed. Tools for this course run through Pixi: `pixi run TOOL` in a project, `pixi exec TOOL` elsewhere. |
| The prompt shows `>` and waits | A quote or a loop is still open. Finish it, or press `Ctrl-C` to start again. |
| Stuck in `less` or `man` | Press `q`. |
| A command runs forever | `Ctrl-C` stops it. |
| You pressed Enter on `rm` too soon | The file is gone unless it was committed to Git. That is one reason to use Git. |

## Apply it to your own mini-analysis

Open a terminal in the folder of your own data. Answer three questions with
the commands from this page: how many files are there, how many lines does
the biggest one have (`wc -l` and `sort -n`), and what do its first lines
look like? Write the commands down: they are the start of your download and
check scripts in [lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd#automate-it).

## Key points

- The shell works in one folder at a time: `pwd` says which, `cd` changes it, and relative paths start from there.
- `>` writes a command's output to a file (replacing it), `>>` adds to it, and `|` passes it to the next command.
- `head`, `tail`, `wc -l`, `grep`, `cut`, `sort` and `uniq -c` answer most first questions about a data file.
- A `for` loop repeats commands over files; a script saves them, starting with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and `set -euo pipefail`.
- Quote variables (`"$f"`), avoid spaces in file names, and remember that `rm` has no undo.

## Further reading

- Cheat sheet: [Bash](../cheatsheets/bash.qmd), with links to the official references.
- **Data Carpentry, *Introduction to the Command Line for Genomics***: the shell for sequencing data, from the same Data Carpentry genomics curriculum as the LTEE data in this course (about half a day). <https://datacarpentry.github.io/shell-genomics/>
- **Software Carpentry, *The Unix Shell***: a general, deeper introduction, with more on loops, scripts and finding files (about a day), and a one-page summary of its commands. <https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/>, summary: <https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/reference.html>
- **MIT, *The Missing Semester of Your CS Education***: lecture videos and notes on the shell, scripting and command-line tools, for when you want to go further. <https://missing.csail.mit.edu/>
- **ShellCheck**, finds bugs in shell scripts (also as a web page): <https://www.shellcheck.net/>
- **explainshell**, explains each part of a command line you paste in: <http://www.explainshell.com/>
- *GNU Bash Reference Manual*, the official manual: <https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/>
